4.1.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why did this hip dislocate?"
- "Four determinants → **design**, **component position**, **soft-tissue tension**, **soft-tissue condition**."
- "The surgeon owns the first three · the patient owns the fourth → a perfect hip can still fail."
- "Commonest surgical cause → **component malposition** · timing points to the cause."

### The four determinants
| Determinant | What it includes |
|---|---|
| **Design** | head size, head–neck ratio, liner, constraint |
| **Placement** | stem position (lateralised tip), **cup inclination**, version |
| **Tension** | femoral offset, trochanter transfer, acetabular offset · GT (greater trochanter) osteotomy failure |
| **Condition** | neuromuscular control → **central, peripheral, myogenic** deficits |

- Check each one in turn → the answer to "why did it dislocate?"
- Patient factors → non-modifiable but can be optimised · surgical factors → modifiable, avoidable

#### Which factor dominates
- **Component malposition** → most important surgical factor, commonest cause (Prof Azzam)
- **Low annual volume** → ≈**50%** more dislocations → the learning curve matters (Prof Azzam)

### Timing, approach & prevention
- Early vs late dislocation → 5 Instability
- **Posterior approach** dislocates most
[[FIG: Fig 4.1 · 4.1
- **Repair capsule + short external rotators** → dislocation 4.46% → 0.4% (Campbell)
#### Prevention
- Prevention starts at the **primary THA** → right patient and implant, restore anatomy, tension soft tissues
- Treating a dislocation always costs far more than preventing it

- **Design · position · tension · condition → malposition commonest → early = position, late = wear**

4.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you put the cup?"
- "**Lewinnek** → inclination **40 ± 10°**, anteversion **15 ± 10°** → most surgeons aim at 40°."
- "Flat cup → impingement, **inferior** dislocation · steep cup → **superior** dislocation."
- "The safe zone is no guarantee → most dislocations happen inside it."

### Stem position
- Stem tip central, valgus or varus on the film → 3 Planning
- **Stem anteversion** adds to cup anteversion → **combined version**

### Cup inclination
- **30–50°** → balanced coverage and range · the range is a compromise
- **<30°** → limited abduction → early neck–cup impingement → **inferior** dislocation
- **>50°** → easy **superior** dislocation
[[FIG: Fig 4.8 · 4.3
- Handbook dislocation page → anteversion error "anterior", flat cup "superior" → this page and Campbell differ

#### The Lewinnek zone and its limits
- **Lewinnek** → inclination **40 ± 10°**, anteversion **15 ± 10°** (Prof Azzam)
- Inside the zone ≠ stable → most early dislocations occur inside it (Campbell)
- Most cups are set at **40°**, not 30° (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 4.9 · 4.3

#### Why the cup ends up outside the zone
- Narrow zone → error with **obesity**, female pelvis, **lateral decubitus**, wall deficiency
- Measured inclination changes with **pelvic tilt** → standing ≠ supine
- **Transverse acetabular ligament** → intra-operative guide to native cup orientation
- Case → inclination ≈**60°** + slightly high centre → recurrent instability (Prof Azzam)

- "Cup + stem anteversion → one compensates the other → aim ≈**25–40°**."
- "Too much → **anterior** escape · retroversion → **posterior** escape."
- "A stiff or flat-back spine defeats a well-placed cup → plan the spine before the hip."

### Version and direction
- **Excess anteversion** → head escapes **anteriorly**
[[FIG: Fig 4.10 · 4.4

[[FIG: Fig 4.11 · 4.4

- Course → **30–50°** · Campbell → **25–40°** (25–45° normal spine) · Miller → 35–40°
- Say → "**combined anteversion ≈25–40°**, higher for a stiff spine (Campbell)"

- **Lateral approach** → stem more retroverted · **posterior** → more anteverted (Prof Gobba)
[[FIG: Fig 4.12 · 4.4

4.5.t: Component Design — Arc, Jump Distance & Constraint
4.5.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does design keep a hip in?"
- "**Primary arc** → range before impingement · **jump distance** → travel to escape after it."
- "A **larger head** improves both · a thin neck adds range but may break."
- "Every rim or lip buys stability with range · **constraint** = salvage only."

### Two margins against dislocation
- **Primary arc** → motion between opposite impingement points → rises with head–neck ratio
[[FIG: Fig 4.19 · 4.5
- **Jump distance** → travel to escape after impingement ≈ **half the head diameter** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 4.20 · 4.5
- **3–4 mm** of jump distance → a major role (Prof Gobba)
- Jump distance falls as **cup inclination** rises → steep cup, less to climb
#### Capsule repair
- Posterior approach → **capsule closed**, head stays · not closed → dislocates

### Head size and neck geometry
- Larger head → more jump distance + more range
- **36 mm**+ → more ROM and stability (Miller) · made practical by highly cross-linked PE
[[FIG: Fig 4.21 · 4.5
- Concern → **trunnion** problems with metal heads
#### Neck geometry
- **Head–neck ratio** → large head, thin neck → more ROM
[[FIG: Fig 4.22 · 4.5
- Thin necks widely made → **neck fractures** after a year (Prof Gobba)
- **Trapezoidal neck** → flattened in one plane → impingement area removed
[[FIG: Fig 4.23 · 4.5
- ROM serves **implant survival**, not sport → extremes → impingement, PE wear, failure
[[FIG: Fig 4.24 · 4.5

### Modifications that cost range
- **Skirted head** (long neck) → thicker neck → head–neck ratio ↓ → early impingement
[[FIG: Fig 4.25 · 4.5
- **Hood / augmentation 20°** → primary arc **100° → 80°** (Prof Gobba)
[[FIG: Fig 4.26 · 4.5
- Hood in the wrong place → impinges early → dislocates the other way
#### Liners
- **Liner offset** → head centre pushed out → longer head travel
[[FIG: Fig 4.27 · 4.5
- **Elevated rim** → where it dislocates → posterosuperior after a posterior approach
[[FIG: Fig 4.28 · 4.5

#### Trading range for stability
- Spectrum → toward range: ROM ↑, stability ↓ · toward stability: the reverse
- **Captive cup** → ROM ≈**60°**, most stable, loosens early in the young (Prof Gobba)

### Constrained cups and their limits
- Liner passes beyond the **head's equator** → locks it in
[[FIG: Fig 4.29 · 4.5
- Neck–rim force → into the **cup–bone interface** and ring → loosening, ring failure
#### Failure
- Case → well for a year → hardware broke, cup moved, superior wall defect
[[FIG: Fig 4.30 · 4.5
- Lesson → no liberal use → **salvage** only

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Arc delays, jump resists · big head, thin neck · every lip costs range · constraint = salvage**

4.6.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you tension a hip?"
- "Restore **femoral offset** and **leg length** → abductors back at resting length."
- "Slack abductor = weak abductor · too much offset → **trochanteric bursitis**."
- "Never buy stability by lengthening the leg → offset is the lever."

### Stretching the abductors
- **Length–tension principle** (Handbook: "Frank-Starling") → force depends on fibre stretch

| Lever | Mechanism | Changes femoral offset |
|---|---|---|
| **↑ Femoral offset** | longer neck or lower neck-shaft angle → trochanter moves away from hip centre | yes |
| **Trochanter transfer** | distal–lateral advancement stretches gluteal fibres | no |
| **↑ Acetabular offset** | lateralised cup → head and trochanter outward | no |

- Trochanteric advancement in practice → 5 Instability
[[FIG: Fig 4.31 · 4.6

### Offset and leg length
- **Offset** → head centre to femoral axis · modular stems adjust it, rarely used
[[FIG: Fig 4.32 · 4.6
- Too small → trochanter strikes → **bony impingement**, instability
- Too large → IT band friction → **trochanteric bursitis**, lateral pain
#### Tension = planning
- Plain "offset" = **medial offset** · + leg length → correct tension
- Tension = planning → component size, position, offset, leg length
- Lengthening for stability → trades dislocation for **leg-length inequality**
- **Long neck**, high offset → minor impingement → levering

### Judging and planning tension
- **Shuck test** → pull the reduced hip distally → watch the head piston
- Neck cut, leg length and templating the offset → 3 Planning

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Offset + leg length = tension · small → impinges, big → bursitis · shuck test · never lengthen**

4.7.t: Hip Biomechanics — Single-Leg Stance & Joint Reaction Force
4.7.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "draw the forces on the hip in single stance"
- "**W** (5/6 body weight) × lever **B** = abductor force **M** × lever **A**."
- "B ≈ 2.5 × A → abductors ≈ **2.5× body weight**, **JRF** (joint reaction force) ≈ **3× body weight**."
- "Lower JRF → medialise the cup, restore offset, lose weight, cane in the opposite hand."

### Single-leg stance
- **W** = **5/6 of body weight** → stance leg below the hip excluded (Orthobullets)
[[FIG: Fig 4.33 · 4.7
- W pulls the free side down → **pelvic drop** · abductors on the stance side level it
- Single stance = **half the gait cycle** · abductors act insertion → origin
- **W × B = M × A** → M = W × (B / A)
[[FIG: Fig 4.34 · 4.7

PITFALL — B ≈ 2A or 2.5A?
- Handbook → B ≈ **2A**, M ≈ 2× · cane example → B/A = **3** · Campbell → **2.5:1**, JRF **3×**
- Say → "**lever ratio ≈2.5 → abductors 2.5×, JRF ≈3× body weight** (Campbell)"

### Joint reaction force
- **JRF** = sum of forces at the hip → seesaw, hip = fulcrum → **Newton's third law**
[[FIG: Fig 4.35 · 4.7
- ↑ JRF → prosthesis wear and native joint degeneration
- Set by **W** and **M** → ↑ B or ↓ A → ↑ M → ↑ JRF
- Running, jumping → up to **10×** body weight (Campbell)

#### Factors raising JRF
| Factor | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Obesity** | ↑ W |
| **Female** | wider pelvis → ↑ B |
| **Lateralised cup** | ↑ B → but abductor stretch ↑ (trade-off) |
| **↓ Femoral offset** | ↓ A → restore it first |
| **Load in the opposite hand** | ↑ B moment · same-side load lowers JRF |

- **Weight loss** → each unit lost removes several units of hip load
- **Anatomical centre** (medial, inferior) → shortest B
- **High hip centre** (dysplasia) → good early, long-term stress → failure (Prof Youness)
[[FIG: Fig 4.36 · 4.7

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **5/6 W × B = M × A · M 2.5×, JRF 3× · fat, female, lateral, low offset raise it**

4.8.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why does a cane help an arthritic hip?"
- "Cane in the **opposite** hand → long lever **C** → counter-torque → abductor force falls."
- "**15%** of body weight on the cane → abductor force **halves**."
- "Lurch = compensation by shortening **B** · **Trendelenburg sign** = compensation failed."

### Trendelenburg lurch
- Lurch → trunk over the weak side → centre of gravity shifts → ↓ B → less abductor force
- Compensation costs energy, looks like a limp · **sign** → pelvis drops, compensation failed
- Abductors → **gluteus medius, minimus, TFL** (tensor fasciae latae) → superior gluteal nerve
- **Antalgic** gait also shortens stance → test abductor power directly

### Cane biomechanics
- Cane → ↓ JRF → ↓ pain, degeneration, wear
- **W × B = (M × A) + (R × C)** → R = cane force, C = cane lever arm
- **Opposite hand** → longest C · same side → almost no lever arm

#### Worked example
| Step | Numbers | Abductor force M |
|---|---|---|
| **No cane** | W 100 N, B 15 cm, A 5 cm → 100 × 15/5 | **300 N** |
| **Cane, 15%** | R 15 N, C 50 cm → 1500 = 5M + 750 | **150 N** |

- **15%** on an opposite cane → abductor force **↓50%** (Handbook)
- W kept at 100 N in the example → a simplification
- Handle at the **wrist crease** · cane moves **with the affected leg**, then the good leg

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Lurch shortens B · sign = failed · opposite cane, 15% → abductors halve**
